coverageDimensions:
SERVICE coverage would mean: of the AWS services that exist, how many can Security Lake natively ingest logs or findings from without a custom source. The page GIVES this, and it is the only coverage claim on the page — 6 services (CloudTrail, EKS, Route 53 Resolver, Security Hub CSPM, VPC, WAFv2) against the full AWS service catalogue. The denominator comes from outside; the page supplies only the numerator, which is correct and sufficient.

REGION coverage would mean: in which AWS Regions Security Lake supports ingestion, and whether any of these six sources is missing in particular Regions. The page GIVES NOTHING. It makes Region a first-class dimension four separate times — the console Regions selector, the required `regions` API parameter, the warning that an unenabled Region returns an error, and the per-Region removal step — and never once names which Regions qualify. The only Region strings present (us-east-1, us-east-2) are placeholders inside CLI examples and must not be read as a supported-Region list. Region coverage for this capability has to come from a different page.

RESOURCE TYPE coverage would mean: which AWS resource types the capability inspects or produces records about. The page GIVES NOTHING, and this is where it is easiest to invent data. The closest text is the "(S3, Lambda)" parenthetical, which names the two services whose CloudTrail data events are captured. Even read generously that is a 2-value sub-list attached to one of six sources, not a resource-type axis, and it must not be promoted into one. Say plainly: no resource-type coverage on this page.

Two further dimensions the page raises but does not populate: source VERSION (a `sourceVersion` parameter and a console Version selector, no version list) and ACCOUNT scope (an `accounts` parameter, with the stated default that omitting it means the entire organization). Both are scoping controls, not coverage.

features.featureName: Collecting data from AWS services in Security Lake (natively-supported AWS services as log sources)
features.reasoning: The page's own sentence defines the set: "Amazon Security Lake can collect logs and events from the following natively-supported AWS services", followed by six bullets. Counted by hand off the page: (1) AWS CloudTrail management and data events (S3, Lambda); (2) Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Audit Logs; (3) Amazon Route 53 resolver query logs; (4) AWS Security Hub CSPM findings; (5) Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) Flow Logs; (6) AWS WAFv2 logs. Six values. Each bullet names one producing AWS service plus the specific log or finding type it emits; the service is the value, the log type is a qualifier on it, so the axis is service and not dataSource — AWS itself calls them services in the framing sentence. The axis is external because the universe of AWS services exists independently of Security Lake, so 6-of-N is a real ratio with a meaningful denominator. This is a single capability, not several: there is one list, one enable/disable mechanism (CreateAwsLogSource / DeleteAwsLogSource), and no second list anywhere on the page that would split it.
features.scope: Per Region and per source version. The page states both dimensions but enumerates neither: the console step says "In the Regions section, select the Regions in which you want to collect data for the source", the API takes a required `regions` parameter and an optional `sourceVersion`, and a Note warns that a Region where Security Lake is not enabled returns an error. No list of Regions and no list of versions appears anywhere on the page.
features.statuses: All 6 are stated as supported, 0 as not supported. There is no Yes/No column, no footnote, no "retired" or "deprecated" marker, and no negative sentence naming a specific unsupported service. The only boundary statement is indirect: anything not on this list must be onboarded as a custom source ("For instructions on adding a custom source, see Collecting data from custom sources"), which is a pointer to another mechanism, not an enumeration of exclusions. So the not-covered side of this axis is empty on this page and must be left empty rather than inferred.

pageTitle: Collecting data from AWS services in Security Lake
shouldNotExtract: The eight IAM actions under "Prerequisite: Verify permissions" (glue:CreateDatabase, glue:CreateTable, glue:GetDatabase, glue:GetTable, glue:UpdateTable, iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole, s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject) plus kms:DescribeKey — these are prerequisites, an axis of API actions you must hold, not things the capability reaches. The JSON policy block. The three API operations named (CreateAwsLogSource, GetDataLakeSources, DeleteAwsLogSource) and their CLI equivalents — an API operation is not a service. Every CLI example and its literal values: sourceName=VPC_FLOW and sourceName=ROUTE53, accounts 123456789012 and 111122223333, regions us-east-1 and us-east-2, sourceVersion 2.0. The console click-paths and the Accounts/Sources navigation-pane steps. The "Tip", "Important" and "Note" callouts about configuring logging, missing parameters and unenabled Regions. The sentence about transforming data into OCSF and Apache Parquet — it is one blanket statement applying to all sources, with no enumeration and no per-source variance, so it is not a fileFormat coverage axis. The entire "See also" section, including the AI-coding-assistant / Agent Toolkit boilerplate AWS now appends to every page. All cross-page links (open-cybersecurity-schema-framework.md, custom-sources.md, subscriber-management.html, the #update-role-permissions anchor).
trap: Reading "AWS CloudTrail management and data events (S3, Lambda)" as three services and emitting Amazon S3 and AWS Lambda as supported sources. They are not sources — they are the two services whose CloudTrail *data events* Security Lake collects, a qualifier inside the CloudTrail bullet. That mistake inflates the count from 6 to 8 and puts two services on the covered list that cannot be enabled as sources. The second trap is scale: the six-bullet list sits in the first ten lines, and roughly 90% of the page is procedure, so a parser that scans for repeated tokens instead of the framing sentence will latch onto the code examples and conclude the supported set is {VPC_FLOW, ROUTE53} — a count of 2 — because those are the only sourceName values that appear more than once. Third: harvesting us-east-1 / us-east-2 from the CLI examples as a supported-Region list, and 2.0 as a version-coverage claim. Fourth: mistaking the eight IAM prerequisite actions for an enumerable coverage axis because they are the longest bulleted list on the page.
whatThePageStates: This page is the how-to for using an AWS service as a log source in Amazon Security Lake. It opens with one enumerable list — the "natively-supported AWS services" that Security Lake can collect logs and events from — and then spends the rest of the page on procedure: the IAM permissions you must hold first, and the console / API / CLI steps to add a source, get collection status, and remove a source. Only the opening list is a coverage statement; everything after it is operating instructions, parameters and examples.
